«...Ce serait vraiment bien d’apprendre: “...It would be really great to learn French, but how can you learn it if you can’t study?”
Depuis son arrivée au pouvoir, le gouver: Since coming to power, the Coalition avenir Québec (CAQ) government has tried several times to reform the province’s economic immigration system. The most recent attempt, announced on July 9, excludes so-called “low-skilled” workers (including truckers, material handlers, orderlies, and agricultural and agri-food workers) from the Quebec Experience Program (PEQ). Those already working in Quebec remain eligible, but they must have a high level of French proficiency before obtaining the Quebec Selection Certificate (CSQ), which is required for permanent residency. According to several workers and immigration specialists, the reform will have serious human and economic consequences. When Donalee Martinez picks up his phone, he is in New Jersey.
Il me dit qu’on pourra se parler le lend: He tells me we can talk the next afternoon, once he is back home in Montréal. In the meantime, he has to cover nearly 700 km to deliver the load of bread in his refrigerated truck. Donalee is part of a group of about 60 truckers of Filipino origin, who are often recruited in the Middle East by agents working for Quebec or Canadian companies. He arrived in Montréal in 2018, thinking that after a few years he could bring over his wife and three children, who were left behind in the Philippines. In his home country, Donalee had run his own trucking company for a few years before trying his luck as a long-haul trucker in Saudi Arabia, where he was approached by a recruiter for a Canadian company.
« J’ai eu la possibilité de venir en Occ: “I had the chance to come to the West and I took it,” he says. “Life is better in Canada than in Saudi Arabia or the Philippines. Here, for example, you know your taxes pay for services that help the community. I like paying my taxes!” With the PEQ reform coming into effect on July 22, Donalee Martinez, like all so-called “low-skilled” workers, will be required to show an intermediate or advanced level of French before he can apply for his CSQ, an essential step toward permanent residency. In the meantime, he will have to renew his work permit every year. He could therefore end up stringing together temporary work permits for years, without knowing whether he will ever be able to settle in Quebec, or whether his next permit application will be refused.
Benito Supan est également camionneur. C: Benito Supan is also a trucker. Like Donalee, he is originally from the Philippines; he too was recruited in Saudi Arabia by a Canadian company.
« J’ai rencontré quelqu’un sur Internet: “I met someone on the Internet who directed me to a job,” he says. “The guy never told us about the permanent residency process, and he never told us we had to learn French either. He asked us for a lot of money, and he promised he would work to get us our residency, that’s all.” To pay the agent who prepared his immigration file, Benito spent about $7,000, the equivalent of more than 10 months of salary. “In Saudi Arabia, they only pay you $600 or $700 a month; you can’t support a family with that. That’s why I wanted so badly to leave,” adds the father of four teenagers. “I would love for my kids to be able to come live with me and finish their studies here.”
Depuis son arrivée à Montréal, Benito vi: Since arriving in Montréal, Benito has lived alone and worked long hours, making round trips between Montréal and Bécancour at the wheel of a tanker truck full of asphalt used for road construction. He has to take French-language courses to have a chance at becoming a permanent resident, but his work schedule barely leaves him time to do his laundry. “We work 10 to 12 hours a day, Monday to Saturday. On Sunday, we go to the grocery store, do our laundry and rest a little. That’s why we don’t have time to go to school. It would be really great to learn French, but how can you learn it if you can’t study?”
« Ça me crève le cœur que le gouvernemen: “It breaks my heart that the government is sticking to its plan for temporary workers,” says Donalee, who has spoken several times at protests against the PEQ reform organized by the citizens’ movement Le Québec c’est nous aussi! He finds himself in the same impasse as Benito. “I would have to pass the French test, but we’ve been working 60 to 70 hours a week since the start of the pandemic. We don’t have time to take courses.”
Pendant quelques semaines, Donalee a pro: For a few weeks, Donalee used his only day off each week to study. “I took a few courses, which I paid for out of my own pocket, but they were cancelled because of the pandemic. At the same time, we were asked to work more on weekends. So I couldn’t continue.”
Pour les futurs travailleurs étrangers,: For future foreign workers, regardless of their level of French, the situation is even more difficult. After July 22, temporary foreign workers deemed “low-skilled” who do not benefit from the grandfathering clause will no longer be able to apply for a CSQ through the PEQ. Immigration lawyer Ho Sung Kim explains that the previous Liberal government reformed the PEQ in 2018 to make it easier to process applications submitted by low-skilled workers.
Les caquistes, qui ont fait campagne sur: The CAQ, which campaigned on reducing immigration thresholds, has for its part tried to reform the economic immigration system four times in a year and a half—starting with a bill that would have outright wiped out 18,000 immigration files in February 2019, then attempting two overhauls of the PEQ in November 2019 and May 2020, before arriving at a final version of the reform in July. “The government is sending a very confusing message with all these reforms. In the end, some people are not affected, but others, even though they have contributed to Quebec society for months, no longer feel welcome.”
Sur l’ensemble des personnes qui ont obt: Of all the people who obtained a CSQ in 2019, 86% came through the PEQ. “The government would like to shut down the PEQ, but it’s afraid to abolish such an attractive program, so it’s making it more complicated,” the lawyer sums up. Asked about this, Marie-Hélène Blouin, spokesperson for the Ministry of Immigration, Francisation and Integration (MIFI), points out that there are other immigration options in Quebec for so-called “low-skilled” workers. Without giving further details, she says the MIFI plans to launch several pilot programs to recruit low-skilled foreign workers, including orderlies and agri-food workers. At the time of publication, nothing had been planned for truckers.
Selon la CAQ, certains travailleurs étra: According to the CAQ, some foreign workers excluded from the PEQ will be able to apply for a CSQ through the Arrima program, which selects candidates based on regional labour needs. The program leaves many people in the field sceptical. For Selin Deravedisyan-Adam, president of the Quebec chapter of the Canadian Association of Professional Immigration Consultants, the Arrima platform is “nothing but smoke and mirrors.”
Selon elle, la grande majorité des trava: According to her, the vast majority of low-skilled foreign workers, even those working in essential sectors, will not be able to go through Arrima. The program uses a points system that favours younger, educated, French-speaking workers. “If a worker doesn’t have [the equivalent of] Secondary V, if their French is limited, or if they’re over 40, it doesn’t matter what their experience is, it won’t work,” explains the consultant. Of all the low-skilled workers who could have gone through the former PEQ and ultimately obtained permanent resident status, she believes only one in 10 could get through Arrima.
La consultante collabore avec des employ: The consultant works with Quebec employers who recruit workers abroad. Since the PEQ reform was announced, she has been making great efforts with these clients to reclassify some workers so they can be eligible for the new PEQ. These clients are mainly in rural areas, and she considers that excluding low-skilled workers from the PEQ is nothing less than “economic suicide” for the regions: “There are villages that, without these families, will not be able to be revitalized.”
En passant par Arrima, les demandeurs re: Applicants who go through Arrima receive a closed work permit that ties them to a specific employer. “That puts them in a very vulnerable situation if the employer doesn’t pay them or if there are other forms of exploitation,” explains lawyer Perla Abou-Jaoudé, a colleague of Kim’s. Benito Supan has already experienced this kind of exploitation. As soon as they arrived in Montréal, Benito and his companions realized their employer was cheating them. “He told us he would pay us $22 an hour, but he only paid $12, sometimes $15. I told our boss he had to pay us the hourly rate written in the contract. He told us that rate was only valid for long trips… but when we went to Ontario, he paid us the same hourly rate as usual. That’s when we filed a complaint.”
Avec le soutien du Centre des travailleu: With the support of the Immigrant Workers Centre (CTI), a community organization in Côte-des-Neiges, Benito and his colleagues obtained open work permits (allowing them to work for any employer) and new contracts. Abou-Jaoudé fears that with Arrima taking precedence, getting open permits will become more difficult, which would force workers to choose between an abusive or corrupt employer, leaving, and going underground.
À plusieurs reprises pendant notre conve: Several times during our conversation, Benito Supan interrupts himself to tell me: “You have to talk to Mister Joey.” “Mister Joey” is Joey Calugay, a Filipino organizer with the CTI. This summer, Joey and his colleagues are criss-crossing Montréal to make migrant workers aware of their rights. He tells his story briefly while handing out flyers at De la Savane metro station, switching between French, English and Tagalog, shuttling between our microphone and the workers passing through, to the rhythm of the turnstiles. He points out that the Filipino temporary workers he works with are “very vulnerable,” not only because of their immigration status, but also because of their limited French and the nature of their work.
« Ils ont souvent les jobs les plus dang: “They often have the most dangerous and dirtiest jobs,” he says. “Yet these are jobs we now consider essential. Our food security depends on them.” “The pandemic has shone a light on these workers’ vulnerabilities… and on the importance of their work,” he says. “It’s time to offer them stability and the chance to stay in the country.”
La ministre Girault a répété à plusieurs: Minister Girault has repeated several times that this PEQ reform will be the last. “Every woman, every man, every child who arrives in Quebec must feel welcomed and at home, and we have a duty to help with their integration. For immigration to adequately meet Quebec’s needs, we must continue to transform and modernize our system,” she said. The PEQ reform did not satisfy the members of Le Québec c’est nous aussi!, who went to the minister’s riding office in Sainte-Agathe-des-Monts last week to hand over letters from workers and students who feel left behind by the reform.
Donalee Martinez n’a pas pu rédiger de l: Donalee Martinez couldn’t write a letter; he was on the road. But he knows what he would have written to the minister: “Give us the chance at residency, and we’ll go to school afterward.” Joey Calugay thinks temporary workers must voice their opposition to the reform. “When we think about things like minimum wage or parental leave, we have to remember that governments didn’t just wake up one day with the idea of granting them to us—these gains are the product of our struggles,” the organizer reminds us. “Our goal is to equip workers so they can make the situation known and fight for their rights.”
Me Ho Sung Kim demande au gouvernement L: Lawyer Ho Sung Kim is asking the Legault government to consult the legal community more. “We don’t want to be fighting all the time,” says Kim, who sits on the board of the Association québécoise des avocats et avocates en droit de l’immigration (AQAADI) and who, along with more than 60 other lawyers, signed an open letter against the reform. “Talk to us. With this reform, there is room for improvement.” He advises workers affected by the reform to seek legal advice.
De son côté, Mme Deravedisyan-Adam conse: For her part, Ms. Deravedisyan-Adam advises employers who are trying to regularize the status of their foreign employees. “We’re working with employers who are trying to maintain the employment relationship with these workers and keep them informed. And we’re working with our candidates to see what’s missing from their profiles. We’re trying to adapt, but this is a reform that sticks in our throats.” Benito Supan and Donalee Martinez, for their part, are thinking about moving to New Brunswick or Western Canada—reluctantly. “I have a friend in Manitoba who told me getting residency there is very easy,” explains Benito. “But if I can stay in Quebec, I’ll stay. It’s the most beautiful place in Canada; and if I can bring my family, we’ll be so happy!”
Mme Deravedisyan-Adam s’inquiète d’enten: Ms. Deravedisyan-Adam is worried to hear workers thinking about leaving. “Many want to leave. If they want to, they can go to other provinces, but I hope there will be a wake-up call before that.”
